lead: A steam power plant burns coal or gas to boil water, spins a turbine with the steam, and condenses the exhaust back to liquid so the loop can repeat. The four devices — pump, boiler, turbine, condenser — form the Rankine cycle. Almost all thermal electricity in India, whether from coal, nuclear or solar-thermal heat, comes from this cycle, so its efficiency decides how much fuel a unit burns for every kWh it sends out.
prereq: You need: Carnot cycle, entropy, the steady-flow energy balance from Unit 1, and steam-table reading from Unit 4 (property tables).

sections.h3: Four devices in a closed loop

blocks.text: Water circulates. The pump takes saturated liquid from the condenser and raises its pressure to boiler pressure; the liquid temperature rises only a little because liquid water is nearly incompressible. The boiler adds heat at almost constant pressure: the water warms to saturation, boils, and is usually superheated. The turbine expands the high-pressure steam and delivers shaft work, so pressure and temperature fall. The condenser rejects heat at constant pressure and temperature, turning the exhaust back into saturated liquid.

For each device, the steady-flow energy balance with negligible kinetic and potential energy gives q − w = Δh. With the state numbers of the figure: turbine work w_t = h₃ − h₄, pump work w_p = h₂ − h₁, boiler heat q_in = h₃ − h₂, condenser heat q_out = h₄ − h₁. Here h is specific enthalpy in kJ/kg, q and w are per kg of water. w_t and w_p are both taken as positive magnitudes — w_t is work delivered by the turbine, w_p is work absorbed by the pump. In the sign convention of q − w = Δh, the pump work is w = −w_p.

A Carnot cycle between the same temperature limits is more efficient, but it cannot be built in steam: compressing a wet mixture needs a huge two-phase compressor running at turbine speed. The Rankine cycle finishes condensation in the condenser and compresses liquid only, which needs a small pump. The price is a lower mean temperature at which heat is added, so efficiency stays well below the Carnot value.

On a T–s diagram the saturated liquid and vapour lines form the dome. Pump work is a short near-vertical line on the liquid side. Boiler heating runs right along a constant-pressure line to superheated steam. Turbine expansion drops down and to the right, often into the wet region. Condensation is a horizontal line at condenser temperature.

The thermal efficiency compares net work out with heat paid for in the boiler. The pump work is small compared with turbine work, but it is real work bought from the same shaft, so it must be subtracted.
η = (w_t − w_p) / q_in = [(h₃ − h₄) − (h₂ − h₁)] / (h₃ − h₂)
blocks.where: η is the cycle thermal efficiency (dimensionless); h₃ is turbine-inlet enthalpy, h₄ turbine-exit enthalpy, h₁ condenser-exit (pump-inlet) enthalpy, h₂ pump-exit (boiler-inlet) enthalpy, all in kJ/kg.

items: Fix the boiler pressure p_b and the condenser pressure p_c.
At the turbine inlet (state 3) take the known pressure and temperature, read h₃ and s₃ from the superheated steam table.
For an ideal turbine, s₄ = s₃ at pressure p_c; find quality x₄ = (s₃ − s_f)/s_fg, then h₄ = h_f + x₄ h_fg.
Pump work for liquid: w_p ≈ v_f (p_b − p_c), with v_f in m³/kg and pressures in kPa, giving kJ/kg. Then h₂ = h₁ + w_p.
Boiler heat q_in = h₃ − h₂, net work w_net = (h₃ − h₄) − w_p, and η = w_net/q_in.

blocks.text: Real machines fall short. Turbine isentropic efficiency η_t = (h₃ − h₄)/(h₃ − h₄s) is about 0.85 to 0.92, so the actual exit has higher entropy, higher enthalpy and more moisture than the ideal one. Pump isentropic efficiency is 0.70 to 0.85, but because w_p is only 1 to 3 percent of turbine work, its uncertainty barely moves the cycle efficiency.

Typical large utility values: boiler at 100 bar and 540 °C, condenser at 0.1 bar where saturation temperature is about 46 °C. The ideal cycle gives roughly 40 percent; with real turbine and pump it drops to about 35 to 38 percent.

items: Reheat: expand in the turbine to an intermediate pressure, pipe the steam back to the boiler to reheat at constant pressure, then expand again to the condenser. The average temperature of heat addition rises, and the exhaust stays drier — quality above about 0.88, which protects the last rows of blades. Efficiency gain is modest, a few percent.

Regenerative feed heating: bleed a fraction of steam from the turbine at several points and use it to warm the feedwater in closed heaters. The boiler then receives hotter water, so q_in falls for the same turbine output. Bleeding removes steam that would have made work, so the gain is real but bounded; practical plants use four to seven heaters.

Condenser pressure: a lower p_c means a lower temperature of heat rejection, which raises efficiency by the Carnot argument. The limit is the cooling water available — river or cooling-tower water near 30 °C — plus air leakage into the vacuum and the length of the last turbine blades.

blocks.text: Raising boiler pressure also raises efficiency, but it pushes the turbine exhaust deeper into the wet region, so higher pressure goes together with superheat and reheat. Supercritical units run above the critical pressure of water, 220.6 bar, where there is no boiling stage at all.

figure.caption: Water goes boiler, turbine, condenser, pump back to boiler. The turbine makes the large work term; the pump work is small but is still subtracted to get net work.

spec.title: Rankine cycle
spec.aria: Water is heated in the boiler, expands through the turbine to make work, condenses in the condenser and is pumped back to the boiler.

examples.question: In an ideal Rankine cycle, steam enters the turbine with h = 3200 kJ/kg and leaves with h = 2100 kJ/kg. Saturated liquid leaves the condenser with h = 200 kJ/kg, and the pump work is 20 kJ/kg. Find the net work, the heat added in the boiler, the cycle efficiency and the heat rejected in the condenser.
steps: Turbine work: w_t = h₃ − h₄ = 3200 − 2100 = 1100 kJ/kg.
Feedwater enthalpy after the pump: h₂ = h₁ + w_p = 200 + 20 = 220 kJ/kg.
Net work: w_net = w_t − w_p = 1100 − 20 = 1080 kJ/kg.
Heat added in the boiler: q_in = h₃ − h₂ = 3200 − 220 = 2980 kJ/kg.
Efficiency: η = w_net/q_in = 1080/2980 = 0.3624, that is 36.2 percent.
Heat rejected: q_out = h₄ − h₁ = 2100 − 200 = 1900 kJ/kg.
Check the energy balance: q_in − q_out = 2980 − 1900 = 1080 kJ/kg, equal to w_net.
examples.answer: Net work is 1080 kJ/kg, heat added is 2980 kJ/kg, cycle efficiency is 36.2 percent, and heat rejected is 1900 kJ/kg.
examples.check:
h3 = 3200
h4 = 2100
h1 = 200
wp = 20
h2 = h1 + wp
wt = h3 - h4
wnet = wt - wp
qin = h3 - h2
eta = wnet / qin * 100
qout = h4 - h1
print(f"{wnet:.0f}")
print(f"{qin:.0f}")
print(f"{eta:.1f}")
print(f"{qout:.0f}")

traps: Using turbine work alone as net work. Subtract the pump work: w_net = w_t − w_p.
Taking q_in from the condenser exit enthalpy h₁. The boiler receives feedwater after the pump, so use h₂ = h₁ + w_p.
Mixing bar, kPa and MPa in w_p = v_f Δp. Convert pressure difference to kPa so that v_f in m³/kg gives kJ/kg directly.
Confusing turbine isentropic efficiency with cycle efficiency. One compares actual with ideal expansion; the other compares net work with boiler heat.
Forgetting that in the condenser the temperature stays constant only while the steam is wet. Once fully condensed, further cooling drops the temperature below saturation.

quiz.q: Name the four devices of a Rankine cycle and state what each does to the water.
quiz.a: Pump raises pressure of liquid water; boiler adds heat at nearly constant pressure and makes steam; turbine expands steam and produces work; condenser rejects heat and turns exhaust back into saturated liquid.

quiz.q: Write the thermal efficiency of a Rankine cycle in terms of enthalpies and state the meaning of each symbol.
quiz.a: η = [(h₃ − h₄) − (h₂ − h₁)]/(h₃ − h₂). h₃ turbine inlet, h₄ turbine exit, h₁ condenser exit, h₂ pump exit, all in kJ/kg.

quiz.q: Why is a Rankine cycle used instead of a Carnot cycle in steam plants, even though Carnot is more efficient?
quiz.a: A Carnot cycle would need compression of a wet two-phase mixture with an enormous compressor. Rankine condenses fully in the condenser and pumps only liquid, which needs a small, cheap pump. The loss in efficiency is accepted for a buildable plant.

quiz.q: Why does lowering the condenser pressure raise the cycle efficiency?
quiz.a: It lowers the saturation temperature T_c at which heat is rejected. The entropy change at rejection, s₄ − s₁, is fixed by the other states, so q_out = T_c (s₄ − s₁) becomes smaller while the turbine work stays about the same. Net work rises for the same boiler heat, exactly as the Carnot argument predicts.

quiz.q: Steam enters a turbine at h = 3400 kJ/kg and leaves at h = 2200 kJ/kg. The condensate enthalpy is 200 kJ/kg and the pump work is 25 kJ/kg. Find the cycle efficiency.
Two plants work between the same boiler and condenser pressures; one uses reheat and the other does not. Explain why the reheat plant is more efficient and why its turbine blades last longer.
quiz.a: Reheat adds part of the heat at a higher temperature, raising the mean temperature of heat addition, so the same heat produces more work. It also reduces the moisture at the turbine exhaust, and dry-ish steam erodes the last-stage blades far less than wet steam.

quiz.q: A simple cycle at 100 bar and 500 °C exhausts to 0.1 bar. Explain why the exhaust is wet, and state two changes that would reduce the moisture.
quiz.a: Expansion from superheated steam at high pressure crosses into the two-phase dome because the saturation temperature at 0.1 bar is only about 46 °C. Superheating the inlet steam to a higher temperature and using reheat at an intermediate pressure both move the exhaust state toward drier steam.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern coal units run supercritical, above 220.6 bar, where water turns to steam without a boiling stage, and ultra-supercritical units push steam to 600 °C and beyond for efficiency above 45 percent. Research in India and elsewhere targets 700 °C alloys for advanced ultra-supercritical plants. Combined cycles pair a gas turbine with a steam bottoming cycle and reach close to 60 percent. Search for supercritical Rankine cycle, regenerative feed heating, and combined cycle power plant.
